steps.premise: Bowls from different makers can look alike once the rack fills.
steps.action: Leave reusable cards and a pencil at the rack so makers can put their names on their boards as they arrive.
steps.consequence: Each board can still be identified after similar work arrives.
steps.quote: Keep a pencil and reusable name cards by the rack so a maker can claim a board before a dozen similar bowls land beside it.

steps.premise: A shelf above a vase can get in the way when a student sets it down.
steps.action: Reserve a bay with enough vertical clearance for tall work.
steps.consequence: The student can put the vase down upright.
steps.quote: Give tall pieces a bay with extra headroom. A student carrying a vase should be able to set it down without tilting it under a shelf.

steps.premise: A shelf can leave too little room to grasp a board that is easy to pick up on a table.
steps.action: Supply boards sized to leave finger room at the edges inside the rack.
steps.consequence: Makers can get a grip on a shelved board to lift it out.
steps.quote: Stock ware boards that fit the rack with room for fingers at the edges, since a board that's easy to lift on the worktable can be awkward to retrieve from a shelf.

steps.premise: Large pots can hide small test tiles.
steps.action: Provide a low tray with compartments for the tiles.
steps.consequence: The tiles stay together where makers can find them.
steps.quote: Offer a shallow, divided tray for small test tiles that would otherwise get lost behind pots.

steps.premise: A maker may be keeping a piece covered until they return to trim it or add a handle.
steps.action: Let the maker clip handling instructions to the board.
steps.consequence: Another student can tell whether to uncover the piece.
steps.quote: Let people clip a handling note to their board when they're coming back to trim or attach a handle. A classmate can then tell whether it's okay to uncover the piece.

steps.premise: Someone carrying work may need to search for an appropriate opening.
steps.action: Keep a table clear next to the rack.
steps.consequence: They can set their load down while they look.
steps.quote: Set aside a clear table beside the rack where someone can put a load down while they look for a suitable space.

steps.premise: Some shelves are too deep to reach all the way across from the front.
steps.action: Keep a way to reach those shelves from behind.
steps.consequence: People can reach the back without leaning over wet rims.
steps.quote: If a shelf is too deep to reach across from one side, leave access behind it so nobody has to lean over a row of fresh rims.

steps.premise: A maker may want one part of a piece to dry more slowly.
steps.action: Keep clean plastic and clips beside the rack so the maker can cover that part.
steps.consequence: The covered area can dry at the slower pace the maker wants.
steps.quote: Keep a basket of clean plastic sheets and clips nearby for makers who want part of a piece to dry more slowly.

steps.premise: An unusually large class project may occupy an entire shelf.
steps.action: Have instructors mark those projects on the studio calendar.
steps.consequence: Other groups can anticipate when that much space will be in use.
steps.quote: Ask instructors to flag unusually large class projects on the studio calendar. Other groups can see when a whole shelf is likely to fill up.

steps.premise: Some people have difficulty lifting a board of pottery above shoulder level.
steps.action: Reserve some rack space within easy reach for them.
steps.consequence: They can shelve their work without an overhead lift.
steps.quote: Save some easy-reach space for anyone who would struggle to lift a loaded board above shoulder height.

steps.premise: After time away, a maker may forget which shelf holds their piece.
steps.action: Give shelves short, visible names that makers can record in their notebooks.
steps.consequence: Returning makers can use the name to locate their piece.
steps.quote: Give each shelf a short, visible name that a maker can jot in a notebook to find a piece after a week away.

steps.premise: In dim light, a low dish at the back of a shelf can look like open space.
steps.action: Aim a small lamp along the back of the shelf.
steps.consequence: A maker can see which spots are free.
steps.quote: A small lamp aimed along the back of a dim shelf makes an empty spot easier to distinguish from a space occupied by a low dish.

steps.premise: On a weekly check, the volunteer needs to know how long boards have been there.
steps.action: Mark each board with its arrival date.
steps.consequence: The volunteer can identify owners to follow up with.
steps.quote: Date the arrival of each board so the volunteer doing the weekly round knows which owners to check in with.

steps.premise: Unclaimed work may be cleared to make room.
steps.action: Agree on how to contact its maker and post the procedure at the rack.
steps.consequence: The maker has an opportunity to collect the piece before its space is cleared.
steps.quote: Agree on a contact procedure for unclaimed work and post it by the rack, giving makers a chance to collect a piece before the studio clears its space.

steps.premise: Beginners may not know how much space to leave when placing pots on a board.
steps.action: Show a sample board on the teaching table with a hand's width of clearance between pots.
steps.consequence: Beginners can see the spacing before loading their own boards.
steps.quote: Leave an example board on the teaching table with the pots spaced for a hand to pass between them. Beginners can see how much room to allow before they load their own.

steps.premise: Carts may repeatedly hit an exposed rack corner during class changes.
steps.action: Place a low bumper at that corner when collisions are common.
steps.consequence: An impact from a passing cart is less likely to jolt the pottery.
steps.quote: Fit a low bumper beside the rack if carts regularly clip its exposed corner, sparing the work a jolt during busy changeovers.

steps.premise: Work that its maker considers finished still takes room on drying shelves.
steps.action: Mark a collection area for the kiln team to receive that work.
steps.consequence: Drying shelves have space for pieces that makers are still working on.
steps.quote: Give the kiln team a clearly marked collection point for pieces the maker considers finished, keeping the drying shelves available for work still under way.

steps.premise: A warped or splintered board can be a bad base for a flat platter.
steps.action: Remove damaged boards from the supply as soon as someone notices them.
steps.consequence: The next student can avoid setting a platter on an uneven board.
steps.quote: Take warped or splintered boards out of the supply as soon as someone spots them, before another student sets a flat platter on an uneven base.

steps.premise: Dried clay can remain on a shelf after a load is removed.
steps.action: Damp-wipe the empty shelf before loading it again.
steps.consequence: The next board has a clean surface and the old clay stays out of the air.
steps.quote: Wipe an emptied shelf with a damp sponge between loads so the next board goes onto a clean surface without kicking dried clay into the room.

steps.premise: A separate lid can be hard to match with its piece once similar lids accumulate.
steps.action: Dry the lid on the same board as its matching piece.
steps.consequence: The maker can find both parts together at the next session.
steps.quote: For a project with a separate lid, keep the two parts together on one board while they dry. The maker won't have to hunt through similar lids at the next session.

steps.premise: A full class may need more room, and repacking delicate pieces is difficult.
steps.action: Provide an overflow rack with the same clearance between shelves.
steps.consequence: Whole boards can go onto the second rack with their pieces still in place.
steps.quote: Offer an overflow rack with the same shelf spacing as the main one so a full class can move whole boards without repacking fragile pieces.

steps.premise: Another person may see damage while the piece can still be repaired.
steps.action: Give that person a way to notify the maker privately.
steps.consequence: The maker can decide in time whether to make a repair.
steps.quote: Give anyone who spots damage a way to leave the maker a private note. The owner can decide whether to repair the piece while there's still time.

steps.premise: A pile of unused boards can look like drying space already in use.
steps.action: Keep spare boards on their own stand by the worktables.
steps.consequence: Students can distinguish supplies from work occupying the rack.
steps.quote: Keep empty boards on a separate stand near the worktables so students don't mistake a supply pile for occupied drying space.

steps.premise: Work may need attention while its maker is away.
steps.action: Let members designate someone to check their pieces during their absence.
steps.consequence: Staff know whom to ask about a piece that needs attention.
steps.quote: Let members nominate someone to check their work during an absence, giving staff a known person to ask if a piece needs attention.
